meta.title: CIRO Retail Securities Exam Syllabus — structured content model
meta.note: Official CIRO syllabus 'Last updated May 8, 2025' (PDF in official/; download URL not yet recorded). Outcome statements condensed from the official syllabus (verbatim-faithful scope: each outcome sentence plus all its 'Consider' bullets/sub-bullets, official terminology kept). Reading-order text extracted per column from the PDF in research/sources/syllabus-raw.txt (the layout-mode research/sources/Retail-Securities-Exam-Syllabus-EN.txt interleaves columns). All 109 outcome IDs and taxonomy levels checked against the PDF extraction on 2026-10-22. Independently re-verified 2026-10-22 from a fresh pdfplumber per-column extraction of the PDF (IDs/order, leading verb = taxonomy for all 109, every Consider bullet and sub-bullet present with no cross-column bleed — incl. column-top continuations of 1.6 and 7.3 — element titles, question counts and summaries verbatim). Taxonomy levels are cumulative (Remember < Understand < Apply < Analyze). Element titles, indicative question counts and summaries are verbatim. Source wording kept as printed, including apparent errors: 5.7 'EFT fact sheets' (ETF); 1.25 'comingling' (commingling); 4.5 'Note for the financial statements' (notes to the financial statements); 5.11 'T-swps' (T-SWPs, tax-efficient systematic withdrawal plans); 8.3 'immediate and cancel' (conventionally 'immediate or cancel'); 6.7 lists 'Fama–French five-factor model' and 'Fama–French five-factor model + momentum' (the three-factor model may have been intended for the first); 4.7 'equity to common share' (unclear ratio); Element 6 summary refers to 'this information' without antecedent. Corrected only: 4.6 'Earning per share' → 'earnings per share'; 4.6 'Efficiency ratio' (heading over five ratios) → 'efficiency ratios'; 7.9 'Claiming all deduction and credits' → 'deductions'; NI numbers 41–101/45–106 printed with en dashes normalised to hyphens (41-101, 45-106). Indicative question counts sum to 120 (27/10/12/14/16/13/14/7/7). Element summaries are our own descriptions of each element's scope (rewritten 2026-10-22 so the file carries no CIRO prose; the official wording is in the syllabus PDF, linked in exam-meta.json).

elements.title: Know-Your-Client (KYC) & suitability
elements.summary: The client relationship at the heart of retail advice: collecting and maintaining KYC information, assessing risk profile, account appropriateness, product due diligence and KYP, suitability determinations, conflicts of interest, outside activities and standards of conduct.

outcomes.statement: Key aspects of the firm–client relationship: the client relationship model; concepts of trust, agency and conflicts of interest; procedures and requirements for working with clients residing in the United States, including snowbirds and other foreign jurisdictions as applicable; considerations for changes in residence.

Importance and content required of KYC information — the client’s financial circumstances (income, liquidity needs, financial assets, liabilities, net worth, whether the client is borrowing to invest); personal circumstances; investment knowledge; risk profile; investment objectives and needs; investment constraints and restrictions (equity, diversity and inclusion considerations; environmental, social and governance criteria; other relevant personal preferences); investment time horizon.

Importance of thorough processes for assessing a client’s risk profile: willingness to accept risk or risk tolerance (including behavioural aspects that can influence it, e.g. preference, knowledge, experience); ability to endure financial loss or risk capacity (financial situation, current investments, investment horizon, need for liquidity); how much risk is needed to achieve the client’s goals or risk need (required rates of return, market risk environment, consequence of failure); resolving conflicts between a client’s expectations and risk profile.
Different types of business structures and their impact on investment opportunities: sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation (private vs. public), co-operative.
The need to accurately document discussions with clients and have the client confirm the accuracy of the information.

Requirements around a trusted contact person in specific scenarios: how to establish a trusted contact person; what this permits and what it does not permit; actions if the client refuses to provide one; when to contact a trusted contact person; how to recognize potential capacity concerns and financial exploitation issues; conditions for using temporary holds; documenting the discussion.
The primary responsibility, prohibition on KYC delegation and obligation to keep KYC information current.

Types of client account records and information collected: verification of identity, account appropriateness assessment, KYC information, acknowledgement of disclosures, record of trusted contact person refusal.
The account appropriateness obligation in specific scenarios.

Key features, advantages and disadvantages of various types of accounts to meet client requirements: advisory (non-managed) account (fee-based and commission-based), managed account, discretionary account, cash account vs. margin account.

Account-related documentation in the account opening process and the amount and type of information collected, considering: the Investment Dealer’s business model; relationship with clients; investment products and services offered by the Investment Dealer; conditions for when to collect one set of KYC information for multiple accounts.
Objective and content of the Relationship Disclosure document: objective, frequency of provision, form and format, content, review.

Importance of containment of confidential information: information barriers and firewalls; grey and restricted lists; the role of investment banking, the research department and corporate finance; cybersecurity; privacy.

Purpose of the required documents in the Investment Dealer’s Welcome Package: fee schedule; CIRO brochures that must or can be disclosed to the client (CIRO Complaints Brochure, How CIRO protects investors, Opening an Investment Account); Canadian Investor Protection Fund; Derivative Risk Disclosure; Investment Dealer conflict of interest disclosures; Investment Dealer complaint handling procedures.
The product due diligence obligation, in specific situations, on the Investment Dealer and on the Approved Person.

The Know-Your-Product (KYP) obligation to all investments purchased, sold or recommended for a client, considering the investment’s structure, features (including initial and ongoing costs) and risks (including impact of costs).
Retail client suitability determination requirements in specific situations: the relationship of KYC to recommendations; the need to avoid excessive switches (churning).
Obligations of the Registered Representative and of the Investment Dealer where client instructions are unsolicited or are not suitable.
Types of investment action for a client’s account in specific situations: purchasing, selling, holding a position, depositing, exchanging or transferring securities.
The difference between the account appropriateness obligation and the suitability determination.
Investment Dealer and regulatory requirements for monitoring and maintaining accounts, including undergoing a suitability determination when there are triggering events.

Potential impact on the suitability determination for a client’s portfolio when relevant changes and updates occur: material change to the client’s circumstances; product and market research; economic, political and social events; emerging issues, financial trends, economic trends and world news.
Regulatory requirements governing the management of conflicts of interest in the best interests of the client, in specific situations: identifying, avoiding, addressing, disclosure.
Requirements relating to outside activities in specific situations: definition, pre-approval, disclosure.

Requirements relating to personal financial dealings with clients in specific situations — prohibition and action relating to: accepting any consideration; settlement agreements; borrowing from clients; lending to clients; control or authority; comingling of assets or funds (business partnerships, investment clubs).

Application of the Investment Dealer’s policies and procedures relating to the management of conflicts of interest: effective controls and qualified supervision; applicable due diligence process for approvals; appropriate record-keeping.
The CIRO standards of conduct in specific situations involving a Registered Representative and their client, or a Registered Representative and their firm.

elements.title: Fixed income
elements.summary: Government, corporate and other debt securities: their features, risks and rewards for issuers and holders, plus bond pricing and yield calculations, duration, and the factors that move fixed-income prices.

outcomes.statement: Regulatory requirements for debt markets: general requirements (to promote fair and efficient debt markets); policies and procedures (the requirement, the content); prohibited practices (obligations on the Investment Dealer, obligations on the Approved Person).
Types and features of fixed-income products: Government of Canada securities, provincial and municipal government securities, corporate securities, guaranteed income certificates (GIC).
Terminology of fixed-income products in specific situations: par value, coupon rate, maturity date, term to maturity, bond price, yield to maturity, settlement, covenants.

Characteristics of fixed-income products: advantages and disadvantages to the investor and to the issuer; sources of risks and potential returns; impact of the costs associated with acquiring and holding fixed-income products.
Characteristics of the following instruments and the conditions that affect their risk–return profile: strips, floating rate, callable/puttable, convertible, extendable, sinking/purchase funds.
Standard calculations of bond yields: income (or current) yield, (approximate) yield to maturity, yield on a zero-coupon instrument, yield curves.

In specific situations, the relationships between: coupon, yield, term-to-maturity and price volatility; Macaulay duration, modified duration and price sensitivity; changes in economic factors and price of fixed-income products.
Modified duration calculation to assess the change in a bond’s price for a given change in yields.

Time value of money in investment calculations: the present value of a fixed-income security given the par value, coupon rate, term to maturity and discount rate; the calculation of any missing variable in a time value of money calculation.

elements.title: Equities
elements.summary: Common and preferred shares and depositary receipts: holder rights, risks and rewards for issuers and investors, prospectus requirements and exemptions, corporate actions, and equity valuation calculations.

outcomes.statement: Requirement for and purpose of a prospectus under National Instrument 41-101 General Prospectus Requirements, and when this requirement may not apply under National Instrument 45-106 Prospectus Exemptions: application to primary and secondary distributions; application to takeovers; comprehensive disclosure; advertising and marketing; timely disclosure requirements; exempt market securities; private placements; accredited investor.
Types and key features of different classes of common shares: dividend rights, voting rights, rights to surplus on dissolution.
Types and key features of Canadian depositary receipts (CDRs): rights to holder, CDR ratio.

Characteristics of investing into different classes of common shares and depositary receipts: source of risks and potential returns; impact of the costs associated with acquiring and holding common shares and depositary receipts.
Features of common share ownership: advantages and disadvantages of common share ownership; advantages and disadvantages to the issuer of common shares.
How corporate actions can affect the shareholder’s position: how dividends are declared, claimed and taxed; the impact of stock splits and consolidations; share buyback.
Types and key features of different classes of preferred shares: dividend rights, voting rights, rights on dissolution.
Characteristics of investing into different classes of preferred shares: source of risks and potential returns; impact of the costs associated with acquiring and holding preferred shares.

The distinction between common share and preferred share ownership in specific situations: advantages and disadvantages to the owners of preferred shares; advantages and disadvantages to the issuer of preferred shares.
Time value of money in investment calculations: the present value of an equity security using appropriate models, including discounted cash flow and price–earnings growth models.

elements.title: Securities analysis
elements.summary: Company and economic analysis for valuing investments: financial statements, ratio calculations and their interpretation, market data and indices, analysis methods, and macroeconomic influences on prices.

outcomes.statement: Factors involved in performing company analysis to determine whether a company represents a good investment: all relevant documents and sources of information; clear explanations of company analysis to retail clients when requested; collaboration and consultation with both internal and external subject matter experts as required, in relation to company analysis matters.

Purpose and content of a company’s statement of financial position: format and items included and how they are classified; purpose of the statement of changes in equity and its relation to both the balance sheet and earnings statement.
Purpose and content of the statement of comprehensive income, including sources of income.
Purpose and content of the statement of cash flows: cash flow from operating activities, from investing activities and from financing activities.
Other factors regarding company financial statements: note for the financial statements; auditor’s report.

Information from basic financial statements to give meaningful responses on the company in question (may involve calculations): liquidity ratios (current, quick and cash ratios); risk analysis ratios (debt to equity, debt to assets, interest coverage); profitability ratios (gross, pre-tax and net profit margins; return on assets; return on invested capital); efficiency ratios (fixed asset turnover, inventory turnover, receivables turnover, payables turnover, working capital turnover); equity ratios (dividend payout, retention rate, earnings per share, book value per share, free cash flow to equity).

Information from basic financial statements to give meaningful responses on the investment in question (may involve calculations): value ratios (earnings per share, price to earnings, dividend yield, dividend cover, dividend payout, equity to common share); the use of trend analysis and external comparisons.
Types and uses of information for equities and fixed income provided by exchanges and regulators: price, volumes, yields and market capitalization; restrictions including cease trade orders (CTOs).

Purpose and uses of market indices: how index values are constructed; index vs. average vs. multi-factor; market-value-weighted vs. price-weighted vs. equal-weighted index; price return vs. total return; asset class, sector, country, international.
Use of indices when providing a market summary and when calculating performance versus a benchmark.

Methods of assessing stock market behaviour: the importance of using different sources of company analysis and company information; fundamental analysis; quantitative analysis; technical/statistical analysis; the assumptions and valuation approaches which may be used.

How industries can be classified into sectors and how these classifications are interpreted in a company’s stock valuation: consumer products, manufacturing industries, service industries, technologies.
Macroeconomic factors to investor expectations of the price of securities and market movements: interest rates, inflation, employment, productivity.
Other factors that impact performance expectations over various time horizons: asset class, volatility, market sector, economic cycle, benchmarks.

elements.title: Managed products and other investments
elements.summary: Managed products compared with direct investing: mutual funds, ETFs, other pooled and alternative products, how they are structured, priced and disclosed, what they cost, and how their performance is measured, including valuation calculations.

outcomes.statement: Types of managed products: mutual fund trusts, mutual fund corporations, income trusts, closed-end funds, real estate investment trusts (REITs), exchange-traded funds (ETFs), wrap funds/fund of funds/ETF wrap, pooled funds.

Main considerations affecting an investor or potential investor in managed products: range of exposures available (income and growth, asset classes, sectors, geography, ethical and ESG considerations, diversification/concentration); advantages and disadvantages of managed products.
Main features of mutual funds: access to mutual funds in Canada; structure (trust vs. corporate); participants – trustee, manager, distributor, custodian; fee structures; daily pricing.

Main considerations affecting an investor or potential investor in mutual funds: advantages and disadvantages to the investor and to the provider; source of risks and potential returns, including risk-ranking methodologies.

Main considerations affecting an investor or potential investor in ETFs: access to ETFs; creation; pricing (market price vs. net asset value (NAV)); ETF management styles; the use of leverage; advantages and disadvantages of ETFs over mutual funds; cost structures.
Features and purpose of fund management styles: active and passive management; smart beta/factor investing; leveraged funds; inverse funds.
Information sources on mutual funds, ETFs and other managed products, including the requirement for the fund fact document and EFT fact sheets.

Typical criteria for the evaluation of a fund’s performance: measuring return (holding period return, money-weighted rate of return, time-weighted rate of return); comparing return (benchmark, peer group).

Methods of valuation for investment in and performance of managed funds (may include calculations): pricing of mutual fund units or shares, including a fund’s net asset value per share (NAVPS); measurement and comparisons of fund performance — standard performance data and total return; use of comparisons and appropriate benchmarks (specified in advance, appropriate, measurable, unambiguous, reflective, accountable, investable).

Impact of costs on the performance of managed products: loads and charges; turnover; taxes (on the fund; on the investor; withholding tax — recoverable and unrecoverable); assessing expense ratios (management expense ratio, trading expense ratio).
Implications of redemptions: tax consequences (T-swps); withdrawal plans; suspension of redemptions – gating.
Factors to consider when deciding between managed products or non-managed products: the investor’s decisions; the Registered Representative’s recommendation.
Types of alternative strategy funds and alternative assets: hedge funds, structured products, alternative investment funds, crypto-assets, private equity, venture capital.

Characteristics of alternative strategy funds and other types of investments: structure; features; fees (management, performance, hurdle rates); advantages and disadvantages to the investor and to the provider; source of risks and potential returns; impact of the costs associated with acquiring and holding other investments; accredited investor requirement.

elements.title: Portfolio construction
elements.summary: Building portfolios: asset allocation, types and measures of risk, short selling and margin, portfolio theory and asset pricing models (with CAPM calculations), market efficiency, and active versus passive equity and fixed-income management.

outcomes.statement: Process of asset allocation decisions: principles of portfolio construction; categories, process and importance of asset allocation; types and key aspects of asset allocation (tactical, strategic, rebalancing, etc.); asset mix categories and strategies for setting the asset mix; the benefits of different stock selection techniques; benefits of a rebalancing strategy; costs of implementation and rebalancing (spread, commission, time).
Different types of risk: interest rate risk, inflation risk, liquidity risk, capital risk, income risk, issuer risk, financial crime risk.
What different measures of risk indicate about an asset or portfolio: standard deviation and variance; beta; multi-factor; drawdown.
Risk management processes to deal with risk and return: the role of risk in asset selection; hedging and diversification; factors that affect the expected return and risk of a portfolio.
Methods of risk management processes to deal with short selling: the process of short selling and the associated risks; margin requirements for long and short positions.

Concepts of portfolio recommendations: modern portfolio theory/mean variance theory; efficient diversification, naïve diversification and industry or issuer concentration; Black–Litterman model; Monte Carlo simulation.

Purpose, advantages and disadvantages of asset pricing models: capital asset pricing model; arbitrage pricing theory; multi-factor models (Fama–French five-factor model; Fama–French five-factor model + momentum; Carhart four-factor model).
The capital asset pricing model to calculate the expected return and risk on a portfolio or asset.
Implications of the efficient markets hypothesis (EMH) on portfolio management.
Active portfolio management techniques for equity managers: top–down vs. bottom–up; sector rotation; growth investing; value investing; market timing.
Passive portfolio management techniques for equity managers: buy and hold; tracking/indexing.
Passive and active fixed-income portfolio management techniques: passive buy and hold; index matching; immunization; duration management; bond swaps; sector rotation.

elements.title: Investment recommendations
elements.summary: Applying the whole syllabus to client situations: matching recommendations to objectives, constraints and risk profile, behavioural biases, goal-funding calculations, Canadian tax planning and tax calculations, and complaint handling.

outcomes.statement: The relationship between a client’s investment objectives and needs, risk profile and performance.

Impact of a client placing non-financial constraints and restrictions on their own investment choices: equity, diversity and inclusion considerations; environmental, social and governance criteria; other personal preferences.

Principles of behavioural finance and the potential impact on a client’s decisions and returns — behavioural biases: cognitive errors (representativeness, illusion of control, confirmation, hindsight); information processing biases (framing, anchoring, mental accounting, availability); emotional biases (loss aversion, overconfidence, endowment); capital market biases (survivorship, gambler’s fallacy, herding, home country).

Retail client suitability determination requirements in specific situations: selection of suitable products; the impact of the Investment Dealer’s product shelf; the client’s net worth and liquidity needs; cash management planning and savings strategies; features of government pension programs.

Relevant processes to choose a portfolio for the client based on their know-your-client (KYC) information: the client’s investment needs and objectives and risk profile; current investment portfolio compositions, risk level and potential shortfall; relevant investment management strategies; solutions to resolve conflicts between a client’s expectations and risk profile; the benefit of cash flow analysis.

Relevant factors in addressing investment actions for a client in specific situations: the impact of significant changes to a client’s KYC information; the potentially unexpected impact of the investment action on the client account (concentration, liquidity); the potential and actual impact of costs on the client’s returns; consideration of a reasonable range of alternative actions.

Key requirements of the investment action recommendation process: the pros and cons of each product and recommended investment action; the risks involved for each product and recommended investment action; what the recommended investment action can accomplish for the client; the process for securing the client’s commitment to the recommended investment action.

Time value of money calculations in setting financial goals for the client: regular investment required to meet a known future objective/liability; regular future income acquired from a single investment (i.e. the present value of an annuity).

Basics of personal and corporate tax planning in investment recommendation scenarios — basic knowledge of tax planning strategies and their advantages: tax preferential accounts and their uses (FHSAs, RRSPs, RESPs and TFSAs); strategies for minimizing tax liabilities (claiming all deductions and credits, income splitting, tax loss harvesting); corporations (active vs. passive income, integration, notional accounts — CDA, RDTOH, GRIP).

Basics of the Canadian capital gains tax system applied to a client’s investment gains: calculation of capital gains and capital losses; tax treatment of gains and losses; strategies for minimizing capital gains tax liabilities.

Basics of the Canadian income tax system applied to income from a client’s investments: calculation of income tax payable; tax treatment of interest; tax treatment of dividends (qualifying, non-qualifying, foreign).
Regulatory requirements governing complaints handling in specific situations: recognition, process, resolution, reporting, prohibited practices.

elements.title: Execution and market integrity
elements.summary: Execution and market integrity under UMIR: recognizing abusive trading, gatekeeper responsibilities, order types, the execution and settlement process, cash and margin accounts, and client confirmations and statements.

outcomes.statement: UMIR in specific situations, covering: best execution; abusive trading (specific unacceptable activities, manipulative and deceptive practices, artificial pricing, improper orders and trades); front running.

Regulatory requirements in relation to the UMIR gatekeeping responsibilities in specific situations: the purpose of the UMIR gatekeeping obligations; the client’s typical financial activity and patterns, to identify suspicious transactions; how to identify and escalate suspicious transactions; possible insider trading activity and violations; applicable regulatory frameworks on whistleblowers; applicable reporting obligations to firms and regulators.
Features of different types of orders to specific client requirements: limit order, market order, immediate and cancel, fill or kill, on-stop orders, iceberg orders, short sales.

Important aspects of the trade execution and settlement process to specific client requirements: awareness of the various marketplaces; placing orders, including processes for handling order errors and changes; the settlement and delivery process; considerations for foreign exchange transactions and currency conversions to facilitate transactions; the purpose and application of the cash account rule; the restriction process on overdue cash accounts.
Use of long and short margin accounts, including special margin situations and the need for specialized trading authorizations.

Reporting requirements to clients: requirements to confirm orders with clients, including fees and commissions; Investment Dealer responsibility for trade confirmations and account statements to be sent to clients.

elements.title: Monitoring, reporting and maintaining client relationships
elements.summary: Ongoing client service: monitoring and measuring portfolio performance (including risk-adjusted return calculations), performance disclosure, communications with clients and the public, and record-keeping requirements.

outcomes.statement: Process of monitoring and evaluating portfolio performance in specific situations, considering the market and the economy and client needs and circumstances.

Process of investment performance disclosure and measurement in specific situations: how performance is measured; how comparative performance is determined; the use of multi-factor regression; the proper use of benchmarks in assessing portfolio performance; transaction costs and tax implications of investment recommendations; fees and charges for the product and the impact on client returns.

Investment performance calculations for individual securities or portfolios over any timeframe: rate of return; absolute risk/standard deviation; risk-adjusted returns (Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen); performance against benchmarks; multi-factor regression.

CIRO requirements when Investment Dealers communicate with clients and/or the public, in specific situations: awareness of obligations and best practices; the appropriate use of professional titles; misleading communications; restrictions and guidelines regarding social media and other communications with the public; off-channel communication issues.

Requirements, in specific situations, to maintain all client responses/records in respect of: account appropriateness; suitability determination; know-your-client (KYC); know-your-product (KYP); conflict of interest; sales practices; compensation arrangements; incentive practices and other compensation arrangements; incentive practices which may benefit the Investment Dealer or Registered Representative.
